as_told.title: Robertson Panel's secret recommendations to debunk, detect and track

tellings.quote: The Panel's concept of a broad educational program integrating efforts of all concerned agencies was that it should have two major aims: training and "debunking."

The "debunking" aim would result in reduction in public interest in "flying saucers" which today evokes a strong psychological reaction. This education could be accomplished by mass media such as television, motion pictures, and popular articles.
That the national security agencies take immediate steps to strip the Unidentified Flying Objects of the special status they have been given and the aura of mystery they have unfortunately acquired;

tellings.page: Part II, Unofficial Investigating Groups, pp. 1416-1417
tellings.quote: The Panel took cognizance of the existence of such groups as the "Civilian Flying Saucer Investigators" (Los Angeles) and the "Aerial Phenomena Research Organization (Wisconsin). It was believed that such organizations should be watched because of their potentially great influence on mass thinking if widespread sightings should occur. The apparent irresponsibility and the possible use of such groups for subversive purposes should be kept in mind.

plain: In 1953 a panel of scientists convened by the CIA, known as the Robertson Panel after the physicist Howard P. Robertson who chaired it, is said to have recommended that the government debunk UFO reports. The former official Karl Nell tells Michels that declassified documents show the panel decided the government should debunk the topic to misdirect the public and "actually infiltrate" the civilian UFO organisations. A Senate staffer named Kurt McConnell tells it too, dating it to 1952 and 1953, naming Robertson and the physicist Luis Alvarez, and adding that the panel, in secret, also recommended ways to detect and track the objects. The panel's own report, dated 16 February 1953 and covering meetings held 14 to 18 January, does set out an educational programme with two aims, "training and 'debunking'," the second to bring "reduction in public interest in 'flying saucers'" through "television, motion pictures, and popular articles." It also urges security agencies to "strip the Unidentified Flying Objects of the special status they have been given and the aura of mystery." On the civilian groups, the report says they "should be watched" and that "the possible use of such groups for subversive purposes should be kept in mind"; it does not say they should be infiltrated. To the tellers, it would mean public doubt about UFOs was shaped on purpose.

discussion.by: Report of Meetings of Scientific Advisory Panel on Unidentified Flying Objects (Robertson Panel), 14-18 January 1953
discussion.text: The tellers do not say which of the panel's papers they mean; in the minutes and the report read here (the declassified text printed as Appendix U of the Condon report) the panel says civilian UFO groups "should be watched" and that "the possible use of such groups for subversive purposes should be kept in mind"; it does not say the groups should be infiltrated.
